lesson.body:
Temperature is like a volume knob for your wine. When a wine is too cold, its smells go quiet and it can taste sharp and grippy, the way a fridge-cold soda hides its sweetness. Too warm, and the wine goes soft and floppy and the alcohol jumps out, a bit like warm beer. The same bottle can taste like two different wines depending on how cold it is.

A rough guide, coldest to warmest: sparkling and sweet wines want to be the chilliest, crisp whites and rosé just a notch warmer, light fruity reds slightly cool (think a chilly cellar), and big bold reds a touch below normal room temperature. You don't need a thermometer. Pull whites from the fridge a few minutes before pouring, and give a red 15 to 20 minutes in the fridge if your room is warm.

The classic mistake is "reds too warm, whites too cold." Most people serve reds at toasty room temperature and whites straight from an icy fridge. Nudge each one closer to the middle and you'll taste the difference right away.
outcomes: Describe how cold and warmth change a wine's taste
Order wine styles from chilliest to warmest serving
Use your fridge to serve reds and whites better

deep_notes: Smells reach you as vapour. Aroma molecules are volatile, meaning they evaporate easily, and warmth speeds that up while cold slows it down. Alcohol is volatile too, so a warm wine sends up a hot, spirity whiff. Cold also changes how your mouth reads a wine: tannin, the drying grip in reds, and bitterness feel harsher when cold, while sweetness seems weaker.

Educators often put rough numbers on this. Sweet wines usually go out at about 6 to 8°C and sparkling at about 6 to 10°C, crisp whites and rosé at about 7 to 10°C, light reds such as Beaujolais at around 13°C, and big reds at about 15 to 18°C. Rich, oaked whites sit in between, at about 10 to 13°C, so their fuller flavours can open up.

A home fridge usually runs at about 3 to 5°C, colder than any wine needs, which is why a white benefits from a few minutes out before pouring. To chill a bottle fast, use a bucket of ice and water, not ice alone: the water touches the whole bottle, so heat leaves much faster. Wine also warms up in the glass, so starting a little cool is fine.

The advice to serve reds at room temperature dates from before central heating, when rooms were much cooler than today. The French term chambré, from chambre, meaning room, described a red rested in a cool room, not in a warm modern flat at 21°C or more. Whites, meanwhile, often come straight from a fridge far colder than they need. Both mistakes hide what the wine does best.

deeper.body: Tannin, the drying grip in red wine, feels harsher when cold. That is why light, low-tannin reds such as Beaujolais, made from Gamay, take a chill well, while big tannic reds like young Barolo or Cabernet Sauvignon are served warmer. As a rule, the more tannin a red has, the less chill it wants.
deeper.title: Tannin hates the cold

v2.body:
Long before central heating, red wine was kept in cold underground cellars. Before dinner a bottle was brought up to rest in a cool dining room and warm a little. The French word for this is **chambré** (say shahm-BRAY), from chambre, a room. That is where the advice to serve reds "at room temperature" comes from. Today's heated homes often run above 20°C, far warmer than those rooms.

Temperature is like a volume knob for your wine. Too cold, and its smells go quiet and it can taste sharp and rough, the way a fridge-cold soda hides its sweetness. Too warm, and the wine tastes soft and flat and the alcohol jumps out, a bit like warm beer. The same bottle can taste like two different wines.

The reason is that smells reach your nose as a gas. The smells in wine are **volatile**, meaning they evaporate easily: warmth sends more of them up from the glass, and cold holds them back. Alcohol is volatile too, so a warm wine gives off a hot, boozy smell. In your mouth, cold makes **tannin** (the drying feel of strong tea), bitterness and acidity (sourness, like lemon) feel harsher, and makes sweetness seem weaker.

A rough guide, coldest to warmest:
• Sparkling, sweet and crisp white wines, and rosé: about 6 to 10°C.
• Rich whites aged in oak barrels and light fruity reds: about 12°C, like a chilly cellar.
• Big bold reds: about 15 to 18°C, a touch below normal room temperature.

So a light red and a rich white meet in the middle. For reds, the rule of thumb is **the more tannin, the less chill**. A Beaujolais, a light French red from the Gamay grape, takes a chill well. A young Barolo, a big Italian red, or a Cabernet Sauvignon has lots of tannin and turns harsh when cold, so it goes out warmer. Cold suits sparkling and sweet wines: it keeps the bubbles lively and stops sweetness from tasting heavy.

The **classic mistake** is "reds too warm, whites too cold". Most people serve reds at warm room temperature and whites straight from a fridge that runs at about 3 to 5°C, colder than any wine needs. Nudge each one closer to the middle and you'll taste the difference right away.

You don't need a thermometer. Pull whites from the fridge a few minutes before pouring, and give a red 15 to 20 minutes in the fridge if your room is warm. In a hurry, use a bucket of **ice and water**, not ice alone: the water touches the whole bottle, so it chills much faster. Wine warms up in the glass, so starting a little cool is fine.
deep_notes: A cellar stays cool all year round. A dining room in a thick-walled house without central heating was only a little warmer. To chambrer a wine was to let it stand in the room where it would be served, so it lost its cellar chill. The idea was always less cold, never warm. In a heated flat the same advice leads you astray, so wine schools now put room temperature for reds at about 15 to 18°C.

Temperature does not change what is in the wine, only how much of it reaches you. The alcohol, sourness, sugar and smells are the same at 6°C and at 20°C. What changes is how many smells float up to your nose and how your mouth reads the rest. That is why the effect can be undone: an over-chilled wine wakes up as it warms in the glass.

Smell happens high inside your nose, where tiny sensors catch molecules floating in the air. Smells reach them in two ways: when you sniff the glass, and from the back of your mouth as you sip and swallow. Both routes need the smell to be a gas, so a cold wine gives your nose less to work with either way. Alcohol evaporates more easily than water, so a warm wine pushes its boozy smell to the front.

Taste researchers have shown that sweetness seems weaker when food or drink is cold. That is why melted ice cream tastes much sweeter than frozen. The same effect helps sweet wines: served cold, a rich dessert wine tastes fresh rather than cloying, meaning heavy and sickly. With dry wines, meaning wines that are not sweet, it runs the other way, since cold also sharpens sourness, the drying feel of tannin and bitterness.

Treat the numbers as a range, not a target. Wine guides differ by a degree or two, and a wine warms in the glass anyway. The order matters more than the figure. Champagne makers often serve their older, finer Champagne a little warmer than young, everyday fizz, at about 10 to 12°C, so its richer smells can show. Rich whites such as Chardonnay aged in oak barrels go out less cold than crisp ones for the same reason.

Gamay, the grape of Beaujolais, makes light, juicy reds with little tannin, the drying feel of strong tea. A chill makes them taste fresh rather than harsh. Pinot Noir, also fairly low in tannin, is often served a little cooler than Cabernet Sauvignon. Nebbiolo, the grape of Barolo, is famous for strong tannin, so a cold Barolo dries your mouth hard. Put simply: the lighter and less drying the red, the more chill it can take.

A home fridge is set at about 3 to 5°C to keep food safe, not to flatter wine. Restaurants make both mistakes too: reds kept on a shelf in a warm dining room, whites left in an ice bucket for the whole meal. It is perfectly normal to ask for an ice bucket for a red, or to lift a white out of its bucket for a while.

Water carries heat away many times faster than air. In a bucket of ice alone, much of the bottle only touches pockets of air between the cubes, so it cools slowly. Fill the gaps with water and the whole bottle is wrapped in cold. A handful of salt makes the ice water colder still. If you use the freezer instead, set a timer: a forgotten bottle can freeze and push out its cork.

deeper.body: Many people chill whites and warm reds simply by colour. Professionals think by weight instead: how heavy and rich a wine feels, and how much tannin, the drying feel, it has. Light, fresh wines of any colour want more chill. Fuller, richer ones want less. So a light Beaujolais and a rich white aged in oak can both go out at about 12°C.

deeper.title: Why fizz and sweet wines go coldest
